Bop
BOP
noun (Gen-Z slang)
Short for bebop, the fast jazz of the 1940s, and from bop, to dance or bounce to music (1950s). A bop for a catchy, danceable pop song has circulated since the 1980s and became a staple of Gen-Z music talk on Twitter and TikTok in the late 2010s ("this song is a bop," "an absolute bop"). Not to be confused with the older verb bop, to hit lightly.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang a bop is a catchy song — the one you cannot stop humming, the one the car sings together. Melody that sticks is a gift: God made the human memory to keep songs better than sentences, which is why Israel was given a hymnbook. The Christian observation: Paul tells believers to let "the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (Col 3:16). He knew what a bop does: it teaches. Whatever a teenager sings two hundred times a week is catechizing him. So the question is never whether a song is catchy but what it is planting. Ezekiel was told the people treated his preaching like "a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice... for they hear thy words, but they do them not" (Eze 33:32); a tune can carry a word straight past the conscience. Amos condemned those who "chant to the sound of the viol" at ease in Zion (Amo 6:5). A father does not need to ban every bop; he needs to give his children better ones — and to show them that a psalm can be sung with joy in the car too. "O sing unto the LORD a new song" (Psa 96:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (from bebop; current since the 1980s, ubiquitous late 2010s) for a catchy, danceable song — and every catchy song is a catechism, which is why Scripture commands psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

expand to see more

BOP, n. (Gen-Z slang; from bebop) A catchy, upbeat, danceable song. "This is such a bop." "Absolute bop."

Bop, v.i. (1950s–present) To dance or bounce to music.

Older unrelated sense: bop, to strike lightly ("bopped him on the head").

Webster (1828) has no entry for bop; nearest root, song: “SONG, noun 1. In general, that which is sung or uttered with musical modulations of the voice, whether of the human voice or that of a bird. 2. A little poem to be sung, or uttered with musical modulations; a ballad. The songs of a country are characteristic of its manners.”

Decode for parents: a compliment to a song. Listen to the words of the songs your children call bops; they are memorizing them.

Key Scripture

Col 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord."

Eph 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;"

Eze 33:32 — "And, lo, thou art unto them as a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument: for they hear thy words, but they do them not."

Amo 6:5 — "That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David;"

Psa 96:1 — "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth."

Modern Corruption

Bop praises catchiness, and catchiness is power: whatever a child sings on repeat is teaching him. Scripture harnesses that power on purpose in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

expand to see more

Music is the most efficient teacher God built into the human frame. A boy who cannot recall last week’s sermon can recite three minutes of lyrics he heard forty times. That is why the word bop is worth a father’s attention: it marks the songs that are doing the most teaching. Ezekiel’s hearers loved his voice and ignored his words (Eze 33:32), and the modern charts have reversed the problem — the words are absorbed precisely because the voice is lovely.

The church’s answer has always been to sing better, not to stop singing. "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly... in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (Col 3:16). Give your children Psalm settings and hymns with tunes that stick; sing them in the car; let them become the family’s bops. A child who has a hundred psalms in his ear will notice when a pop song is lying to him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Bebop (1940s jazz) → bop, to dance (1950s) → a bop, a catchy song (1980s) → Gen-Z music praise (late 2010s).

expand to see more

Bebop — imitative jazz term, 1940s

1950s: bop, to dance or move to music

1980s–present: a bop, a catchy, danceable song

Late 2010s Twitter / TikTok: "an absolute bop"

Distinct from bop, to hit lightly

Usage

""Put that one on again, it’s a bop.""

"Every bop is a catechism; choose which one your children learn (Col 3:16)."

"Give them psalms catchy enough to become the family’s bops."
